tx.t: This lecture looks at the history and the future of electric cars. Electric vehicles are older than many people think. The first ones appeared in the eighteen thirties.
Around the year nineteen hundred, more than a quarter of the cars on American roads were electric. Petrol cars then became cheaper and could travel further, so electric cars almost disappeared.

Modern electric cars use lithium-ion batteries, which store more energy for their weight. Their main advantage is that they produce no exhaust gases while driving, though making the batteries does cause pollution.

Why did electric cars almost disappear?

qs.q: What kind of batteries do modern electric cars use?

tx.t: Today I would like to talk about the history of the Olympic Games. The ancient Games began in seven hundred and seventy-six BC at Olympia in Greece.

They were held every four years for about twelve centuries, until they were banned in the late fourth century. The modern Games were revived in eighteen ninety-six in Athens, mainly through the efforts of a Frenchman, Pierre de Coubertin.
Women first took part in the Games in nineteen hundred, in Paris. The first Winter Games were held in nineteen twenty-four at Chamonix, in France.
Today, thousands of athletes from more than two hundred countries compete in the summer Games.

tx.t: Today I would like to describe a bike-sharing scheme in the town of Calder. It began in twenty fourteen with four hundred and sixty-six bikes, placed at stations around the centre.
Use grew quickly. Within three years the number of journeys had risen by fifty-two per cent, and on a busy day there were more than thirty thousand trips.
The scheme soon met a serious problem: theft and damage. The council solved it with a tracking system fixed inside each frame.
Today, a ride costs one pounds eighty for the first half hour, and the first fifteen minutes are free for residents.

tx.t: This lecture is about the short history of the internet. The first network, ARPANET, linked four American research sites in nineteen sixty-nine.

In nineteen seventy-one, Ray Tomlinson sent the first email between computers and chose the at sign for addresses. Tim Berners-Lee, a British scientist working at CERN, invented the World Wide Web at the end of the nineteen eighties.

The web and the internet are not the same thing: the internet is the network, and the web is one service that runs on it. Google was founded in nineteen ninety-eight by two students at Stanford University.
Today, more than five billion people use the internet.

qs.q: How many sites did ARPANET first link? ____

tx.t: Researchers at the University of Alderton carried out a study in twenty seventeen to find out how students prepare for exams. They followed one hundred and seventy-seven students over six weeks.
On average, the students studied for four hours a day. However, only fifty-one per cent of them used any planned method.

The students who used the method of studying in short sessions with breaks remembered more of the material a week later. The researchers concluded that how you study may matter more than how long you study.

tx.t: In this lecture I will talk about the Great Wall of China. The wall was not built at one time. Different rulers built and rebuilt sections over more than two thousand years.

The first emperor of China, Qin Shi Huang, joined earlier walls together around two hundred and twenty-one BC. Most of the wall that tourists visit today was built in the Ming dynasty, from stone and brick.

A survey in two thousand and twelve measured all its sections at more than twenty-one thousand kilometres. It is a popular story that the wall can be seen from space with the naked eye, but this is not true.

tx.t: Today I would like to outline what glaciers are, and why they matter for sea level. Glaciers cover about ten per cent of the world's land area.
Together, glaciers and ice sheets store about two thirds of the world's fresh water. A glacier forms when snow builds up for many years and is pressed into dense ice.
Since nineteen hundred, the global sea level has risen by about twenty centimetres. This rise is caused partly by melting ice and partly because warm water takes up more space.
